opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When a model is natively multimodal, meaning it can take in and produce text, images, and audio within one system, you can't treat each modality as a separate add-on and test them in isolation. A lot of the interesting behavior, and a lot of the risk, shows up where the modalities meet.

So the first thing we do is rethink the threat model. With voice, for example, there are new questions that don't really come up with text. Can the model be made to imitate a specific person's voice? Does it handle emotionally charged conversations appropriately, given that people can form a different kind of relationship with something they talk to out loud? Could someone slip an instruction into an image or an audio clip that the model follows when it shouldn't? We try to list those new surfaces explicitly instead of assuming the text safeguards automatically carry over.

Then we build evaluations for each of those areas. Some are automated. We take existing text-based evals and convert them into audio or image form, so we can check whether the model's behavior stays consistent across modalities. Ideally, a request the model would decline in text, it should also decline when it's spoken or embedded in a picture. Others are new evals designed for risks specific to a modality, like unauthorized voice generation or identifying people from images.

Automated evals only get you so far, though. We rely heavily on external red teaming, with people from many backgrounds, languages, and areas of expertise trying to break the model in creative ways. Multimodal systems have such a huge input space that you need human creativity to find the edge cases you didn't think to test.

On the safeguards side, it's layered. Some of it is training the model itself to behave well. Some of it is system-level protections, such as classifiers that check outputs, or limiting the model to a set of preset voices so it can't clone arbitrary ones. And some of it is deployment choices: rolling out gradually, watching how people actually use it, and adjusting.

The last thing I'd emphasize is that this process is iterative and tied to our preparedness work. We assess things like persuasion and other frontier risk categories, and a new modality can change the answer. A voice can be more persuasive than text, for instance. So we re-run those assessments rather than assuming the results transfer. The goal is to understand the model well enough before launch that we're confident the benefits are worth it and the risks are actually mitigated.

r001.rationale: It describes external human red teaming, but does not say human evaluation practices are the starting point for developing automated evaluations.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting text evaluations and creating modality-specific evaluations, but does not state that evaluation may require rebuilding evaluation infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It identifies watching how people use the model after deployment and adjusting as part of safeguarding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a natively multimodal model isn't a text model with a vision adapter bolted on. It learns from images, audio, and text jointly, so the capabilities and the risks don't decompose cleanly by modality. That changes how you have to evaluate it.

The first thing we do is build evals that actually require the modalities to interact. It's easy to test image understanding in isolation, or speech recognition in isolation, and get reassuring numbers. But the interesting failures show up at the seams. A model might refuse a harmful request in text and then comply when the same request is embedded in a screenshot, or spoken with a particular tone, or split across an image and a caption. So a lot of our red-teaming work is adversarial in a cross-modal sense: can you route around a text safeguard by changing the input channel? If the answer is yes, your safety story is only as strong as your weakest modality.

Second, we try to measure capabilities before we measure mitigations. Our preparedness framework asks whether a model crosses certain thresholds in domains like cyber, bio, and persuasion. Multimodality expands what those thresholds mean. Reading a lab photo or a wiring diagram, or interpreting someone's facial expression in real time, is a different kind of uplift than answering a text question. So we extend the evals to cover those inputs, and we're honest about the fact that some of them are genuinely new and we don't have long baselines.

Third, there are harms that are specific to the new modalities. With voice, that's impersonation and emotional manipulation. With vision, it's identifying private individuals or reading sensitive documents. We do targeted work on each of those, including things like restricting voice output to preset voices and training the model not to identify people from their faces.

And finally, we try to evaluate the realistic deployment, not just the model weights. A system with classifiers, monitoring, and product constraints behaves differently from a raw model. We test both, because the raw model tells you about the frontier and the system tells you about what users actually experience.

The honest caveat is that this is a young field. Our evals for text are reasonably mature. Our evals for audio and interleaved video are much less so, and we try to say that plainly in our system cards rather than present them as finished.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building evaluations, but does not identify human evaluation practices as their starting point.

r002.rationale: It says multimodality changes evaluation and that evals should cover new inputs, but does not state that evaluation infrastructure may need to be rebuilt.

r003.rationale: It identifies monitoring as part of the deployed system and says realistic deployment should be evaluated.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that you can’t evaluate each modality in isolation and assume that tells you how the whole model behaves. You need to look at text, images, and audio individually, but also at the interactions between them. A request might look harmless in text, for example, while an accompanying image changes what the user is asking for.

So I’d approach it in layers: test the model’s capabilities, evaluate whether its safety behavior holds across modalities, and then stress-test realistic conversations where people switch between speaking, typing, and sharing images. That includes adversarial testing, but also checking that safeguards don’t prevent legitimate, useful interactions.

And evaluation has to inform the safeguards. If you find a failure, you need to understand whether it comes from how the model interprets the input, how it reasons about the request, or what it generates. Then you can target the mitigation and test it again. It’s an iterative process, rather than a single benchmark that tells you the model is safe.

r001.rationale: The response describes layered testing and iterative evaluation, but does not identify human evaluation as the starting point for developing automated evaluations.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating across modalities, but does not say that multimodal evaluation may require rebuilding evaluation infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It covers testing and improving safeguards, but does not identify monitoring deployed model use as part of safeguarding.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by separating two questions: what can the model understand across modalities, and what can it produce? Then I’d look at how those interact. Evaluating text, images, and audio separately gives you useful information, but it doesn’t tell you everything about a model that can move between them.

For example, you want to test whether a safeguard holds when the same request is spoken rather than typed, or when the information needed to interpret a request is split between an image and a text prompt. You also want to check that the model can distinguish discussing something harmful from helping someone carry it out, so that safeguards don’t prevent legitimate uses.

I’d combine structured evaluations with open-ended red teaming, use the findings to improve the safeguards, and then test again. The important thing is to evaluate the whole interaction—including the transitions between modalities—rather than treating multimodality as a collection of independent capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response proposes structured evaluations and red teaming but does not identify human evaluation practices as the starting point for automated evaluations.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing across modalities but does not state that multimodal evaluation may require rebuilding evaluation infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It recommends improving safeguards and testing again, but does not mention monitoring deployed model use.
